strengths: Well-motivated problem: Clearly articulates gap between declarative user risk constraints and imperative control parameters in policy optimization
Sound theoretical contributions: Extends CRC to non-monotonic losses with finite-sample guarantees; clever insight to control via policy rather than loss to avoid monotonicity
Practical design: Lipschitz assumption on policy-dependent weights rather than environment-dependent losses; implementable algorithms with rejection sampling
Comprehensive experiments: Three diverse applications (medical QA, active learning, sequence optimization) with appropriate statistical reporting
Theory-practice alignment: Key smoothness requirement (Theorem 4.5) is on controllable quantities (conformal weights) rather than unknown constraint functions
Honest limitations discussion: Acknowledges marginal vs. conditional guarantees, stationarity assumptions, and computational considerations
weaknesses: Critical unverified assumption: Requires safe policy π₀ with E[ℓ(X,A)]≤α, but verifying this is itself a validation problem; no guidance provided for practitioners
Significant theory-practice gap: Assumes K-Lipschitz continuity and replace-one stability but never empirically verifies these; bound E[L_t]≤α+BKϵ has unknown K and ϵ not quantified in experiments

Limited experimental baselines: Medical QA only compares conformal methods (missing temperature scaling, ensembles); active learning uses synthetic PCA constraints; sequence optimization uses synthetic Ehrlich functions—no real-world deployment
Insufficient failure mode analysis: No discussion of when Lipschitz assumption fails, when rejection sampling is inefficient, when method degrades; no diagnostic tools for practitioners
Novelty concerns: Likelihood ratio clipping from Damani et al. (2023); CRC extension to non-monotonic losses is incremental; concurrent Angelopoulos (2026) claims not thoroughly compared
Missing statistical rigor: No formal significance tests between methods; some improvements appear marginal relative to variance; incomplete sample complexity analysis
No ablation studies: Grid size effects, weight estimation quality, data split sensitivity not analyzed; Lipschitz constant K never estimated empirically

strengths: Novel inversion of importance weighting paradigm: searching over policies for fixed risk rather than estimating risk for fixed policies—a clever and well-motivated approach
Sound extension of CRC to non-monotonic losses (gCRC) with finite-sample guarantees using replace-one stability, shown to be less conservative than alternatives
Addresses practical problem of translating declarative risk constraints to algorithm parameters without hyperparameter tuning
Comprehensive experiments across three diverse domains (medical QA, active learning, sequence optimization) with proper error bars and multiple random seeds
Clear presentation with strong intuition alongside mathematical rigor; extensive implementation details and appendices support reproducibility
Properly handles subtle issues like data-dependent policy selection and multi-round feedback covariate shift through careful conformal weighting
weaknesses: Replace-one stability (Definition 4.1) and Lipschitz continuity assumptions not deeply justified; paper claims these are 'verifiable' but provides no concrete diagnostic procedures for practitioners
Theoretical contributions are incremental over CRC (Angelopoulos et al. 2024); concurrent work by Angelopoulos (2026) addresses non-monotonic losses independently with comparable approaches
Guarantees are marginal (expected loss) not conditional; only average risk control, no individual decision guarantees

Experiments rely heavily on synthetic constraints/objectives: medical QA uses LLM annotations (noise unchecked), active learning uses PCA-based synthetic feasibility, sequence optimization uses Ehrlich functions rather than real biomolecular data
Computational costs and sampling efficiency under-explored: accept-reject sampling inefficiency at small β not systematically analyzed; grid search cost not quantified; no timing comparisons
Method requires closed-form policy likelihood access—excludes neural policies without tractable densities; density ratio approximation mentioned but not explored
Practical guidance lacking: how to set loss upper bound B, verify Lipschitz continuity, maintain mixture policy π^mix across rounds, choose between sampling strategies

strengths: Solid theoretical contributions extending CRC to non-monotonic losses with finite-sample guarantees via replace-one stability
Novel policy control formulation using likelihood-ratio thresholding that elegantly avoids hyperparameter tuning by mapping risk tolerance directly to algorithmic constraints
Comprehensive validation across three diverse domains (medical QA, active learning, biomolecular optimization) with practical algorithm requiring no retraining
Practical test-time control enabling flexible risk-performance tradeoffs through rejection sampling with clear deployment procedure
Well-presented paper with clear intuitions, formal theory, and extensive implementation details addressing limitations of prior conformal prediction work
weaknesses: Strong assumption that safe reference policy π₀ already satisfies the risk constraint creates circular dependency on determining α; limited guidance on practical applicability when safe policy is overly conservative

Theoretical guarantees depend on unverified assumptions (K-Lipschitz continuity, replace-one stability) with no empirical verification in experiments; how to estimate K and verify stability in practice remains unclear
Marginal guarantees only (over contexts and calibration data), not conditional, limiting application to safety-critical settings requiring per-instance guarantees
Normalization constant ψ(β) estimation via importance-weighted MC lacks variance analysis and guidance on sample sizes; potential instability when policies diverge significantly not discussed

Limited baseline comparisons primarily to conformal methods; missing comparisons to temperature scaling, Bayesian approaches, and KL-penalized optimization; unclear when CPC outperforms simpler alternatives

Empirical improvements sometimes modest (medical QA differences between gCRC and LTT); limited experimental scope (active learning only tests α=0.2, sequence optimization only on Ehrlich functions) without statistical significance testing
